title: gpu-node-image-supply-chain-and-multi-account-iac-pipeline
author: Diego Morales
content:
Overview

This document describes the end-to-end supply chain for GPU node images and the multi-account IaC pipeline used at Redwood Inference. It covers Terraform module patterns for multi-account networking and instance profiles, the CI/CD pipeline used to build and sign GPU node images, canary promotion and observability guardrails, and an operational runbook for image-related incidents. The goal is to ensure secure, auditable, and low-risk image promotion across cloud accounts (dev/stage/prod) and on-prem clusters.

Goals

- Provide a repeatable, auditable image build and promotion workflow that minimizes blast radius for GPU node updates.
- Ensure images are cryptographically signed and verifiable by all accounts.
- Keep promotion latency low (target: < 6 hours from build to full prod rollout for urgent fixes).
- Automate multi-account Terraform promotion with gating and rollback.

Scope and Non-Goals

In scope:
- Terraform modules and deployment pipeline for node images and instance profile bootstrap.
- CI pipeline for image build, tests, signing, and promotion.
- Monitoring dashboards and alert thresholds for canaries.

Out of scope:
- Application-level configuration inside user containers (handled by product teams).
- Hardware procurement and physical maintenance (handled by ops hardware team).

High-level architecture

1) Image Build Account (CI): builds AMIs/VM images and produces artifacts (image ID, SBOM, signatures).
2) Artifact Registry (S3/OCI): stores images metadata, SBOM, and signatures in an immutable path with object locking lifecycle.
3) Promotion Orchestrator (GitOps/Terraform): applies image references into per-account Terraform state with strict gating.
4) Target Accounts (dev, stage, prod): receive promotion via a controlled pipeline that updates launch templates / machine pool specs.

Diagram (text):

[CI Build] --> [Artifact Registry (s3://redwood-images/<date>/)] --> [Promotion Orchestrator (pipeline)] --> [Target Account A (dev)] --> [Target Account B (stage)] --> [Target Account C (prod)]

Terraform modules and patterns

We follow a composition-first module design. Key modules:

- module.networking.shared-vpc (reused across accounts)
- module.instance-profiles.gpu-node (IAM, policies, encrypted keys)
- module.images.promoted-reference (single source of truth for image metadata and signatures)
- module.machine-pool.gpu-autoscale (launch templates, node taints, kube labels)

Recommended usage example (consumer stack):

```
module "gpu_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo/internal-terraform//modules/machine-pool/gpu-autoscale?ref=v1.8.0"
  cluster_id = local.cluster_id
  instance_type = "p4d.24xlarge"
  launch_template_image = module.promoted_image.image_id
  instance_profile = module.instance_profile.name
  node_taints = ["workload=ml:NoSchedule"]
  tags = { team = "inference", env = var.env }
}
```

Table: module responsibilities and requirements

| Module | Responsibility | Inputs (required) | Outputs |
|--------|----------------|-------------------|---------|
| promoted-reference | Holds image metadata and expected signature | image_id, sbom_path, gpg_sig_path | image_id, signed_by, sbom_url |
| gpu-autoscale | Launch template lifecycle + ASG/Karpenter hooks | image_id, instance_profile | node_pool_id, lt_id |
| instance-profile | IAM, KMS, instance roles for nodes | account_id, kms_key | instance_profile_name |

Secure signing and SBOM policy

- Every image build produces: AMI/VM image ID, SBOM (CycloneDX JSON), and a GPG sig of the image metadata bundle.
- Signing keys are held in the CI account HSM/KMS. A public verification key is published to a central keyring in the Artifact Registry.
- The signer produces a file: metadata.json + metadata.json.sig. Promotion is blocked if signature verification fails.

Example sign and verify commands used in CI (simplified):

```
# Sign metadata (CI build account)
gpg --output metadata.json.sig --detach-sign --local-user ci@redwood.internal metadata.json
aws s3 cp metadata.json s3://redwood-images/2025-01-10/metadata.json
aws s3 cp metadata.json.sig s3://redwood-images/2025-01-10/metadata.json.sig

# Verify (promotion step)
gpg --verify metadata.json.sig metadata.json
```

CI/CD pipeline: stages and gates

Pipeline (high-level stages):
1) build-image: bake GPU image, run zero-touch kernel and driver tests, generate SBOM.
2) unit-smoke: boot small VM, validate nvidia-smi, run micro-benchmarks.
3) integration-eval: run a small inference eval harness against test endpoints (10k tokens).
4) sign-and-publish-artifact: sign metadata, upload to registry.
5) canary-deploy (dev->stage): apply Terraform to a canary pool (5–10 nodes).
6) observability-gates: verify GPU registration time, driver crash rates, eviction rates, and end-to-end tail latency.
7) progressive-promotion: stage->prod partial rollout (5% -> 25% -> 100%) with manual approvals.

A minimal GitLab CI YAML snippet (illustrative):

```
stages:
  - build
  - test
  - sign
  - promote

build-image:
  stage: build
  script: ["./build-image.sh"]

sign-and-publish:
  stage: sign
  script: ["./sign-metadata.sh"]
  rules:
    - if: $CI_COMMIT_TAG

canary-deploy:
  stage: promote
  script: ["./promote.sh --env stage --canary 5"]
  when: manual
```

Promotion policy and approvals

- Any promotion from build->stage is automated after passing tests.
- Promotion from stage->prod requires:
  - Auto gates green for 24 hours on stage (for routine releases).
  - For safety-critical or non-backwards compatible kernel/drivers: 2 approvers from infra-sre + one product owner.
- Emergency hotfix flow: manual approval from infra-oncall is sufficient; promotion must be marked with an incident ID and SBOM snapshot.

Canary guardrails and thresholds

Metric guardrails (sample):
- Node registration time: < 90s (warn if > 60s, critical if > 120s).
- GPU driver crash loop count per node: < 0.1/h (critical > 1/h).
- Pod eviction rate on new nodes: < 0.5% per hour.
- 95th percentile inference tail latency change vs baseline: < +15% (critical > +30%).
- Failure budget: no more than 1 failed canary deployment per month for a given image family.

Monitoring and dashboards

- Dashboards: "GPU Node Health (canary)" per account with the above KPIs, plus SBOM verification status.
- Alerts: send to #infra-canaries Slack and create PagerDuty incident on critical thresholds.
- Traces: correlate kernel oops and driver logs via distributed tracing linking image_id metadata.

Rollout and rollback procedures (operational)

1) Canary deploy to 5% of capacity in prod (where applicable) or to a dedicated canary ASG of 5 nodes.
2) Observe for 2 hours on automated gates or longer for major kernel changes (24h).
3) If any critical threshold breaches: execute rollback.

Rollback steps (numbered):
1. Trigger Terraform apply using the previous promoted-reference image_id (artifact path is immutable).
2. Scale down canary ASG or patch machine pool to remove new nodes: `terraform apply -var image_id=ami-previous`.
3. Verify all pods drain and reschedule to old nodes. Check node taints/labels.
4. Open an incident, attach SBOM diff, and mark the image as quarantined in the registry.
5. Re-run CI build/test to triangulate root cause.

Quick rollback CLI examples:

```
# Promote back to previous image in account
cd infra/overlays/prod
terraform init
terraform apply -var "promoted_image_id=ami-2024abcd1234" -auto-approve
```

Incident runbook: image-caused node instability

- Symptoms: sudden spike in driver crashLoop, node reboots, or regression in tail latency after an image rollout.
- PagerDuty: infra-oncall -> escalate to runtime-team if driver / kernel issues.

Immediate actions (first 15 minutes):
- Pause further promotions in the pipeline (cancel jobs).
- Trigger rollback to the last-known-good image (see rollback steps).
- Collect crash logs: dmesg, journalctl, /var/log/nvidia-installer.log, SBOM and signature files.
- Tag the artifact in the registry with `quarantine/<image_id>` and set a retention flag for forensic analysis.

Post-incident (postmortem template):
- Summary of impact (nodes affected, start/end time).
- Image metadata and SBOM.
- Root cause analysis and remediation plan.
- Action items (owners and due dates).

Operational ownership and contacts

- Image build pipeline owner: Diego Morales (infra-image-team).
- Promotion orchestration and Terraform modules: Asha Patel (infra-iac).
- Oncall escalation for runtime issues: infra-oncall rotation (see internal rota page).
- Security / signing: Security Eng (Ravi Singh) — maintains keyring and KMS policies.

Audit and compliance notes

- All promotions are recorded in the artifact registry with an append-only log (S3 object lock + CloudTrail).
- Promotion approvals are captured as Git commits/PRs in the promotion overlay repo; PRs must include link to SBOM and signature verification output.
- Retain SBOMs and signatures for 3 years for compliance.

Appendices

A — Common failure modes and quick checks
- Failed signature verification: check key rotation and CI signer logs.
- Kernel panic on boot: compare kernel version & driver modules in SBOM with node runtime.
- High eviction rate: check kubelet logs and cluster autoscaler interaction; verify instance types and interruptibility.

B — Example SBOM check (cyclonedx jq filter)
```
jq '.components[] | select(.type=="library") | {name, version, purl}' sbom.json
```

C — Useful links
- Image Registry: s3://redwood-images (internal)
- Promotion overlay repo: git@repo:infra/promotion-overlays.git
- Oncall rota: /confluence/eng-infra/oncall-and-incident-response

End of document
